nameStory: The 'little glassywing' gets its charming name from the small, translucent patches on its wings that look like tiny windows of frosted glass. These clear spots catch the light as the butterfly darts through meadows, creating brief flashes that seem almost magical. The 'little' part distinguishes it from other glassywing skippers that are larger.
description: The little glassywing is a small, fast-flying butterfly in the skipper family, known for their quick, darting flight patterns. With a wingspan of just over an inch to about an inch and a half, it's one of the smaller skippers you'll encounter in New England. The wings are typically brown with those distinctive translucent 'windows' that give it its name. Like other skippers, it has a stocky body and relatively small wings compared to other butterflies.

idTips.label: Translucent wing spots
idTips.description: Look for small, clear patches on the wings that look like tiny panes of glass - these catch sunlight and create a distinctive glinting effect as the butterfly moves

idTips.label: Size and wingspan
idTips.description: Small butterfly with wings spanning just over an inch to about 1.5 inches - noticeably smaller than many other butterflies in the same habitats

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Quick, darting, erratic flight typical of skippers - they seem to 'skip' through the air rather than glide smoothly like other butterflies

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Stocky, robust body that looks thick compared to the relatively small wings - gives them a compact, almost moth-like appearance

idTips.label: Color preference when feeding
idTips.description: Shows a strong preference for white, pink, and purple flowers - you'll often find them on mint, dogbane, and joe-pye weed blossoms

habitat: Little glassywings prefer open, sunny areas with abundant wildflowers, especially meadows, prairies, and field edges where native grasses grow. They're particularly drawn to areas with purpletop grass, which their caterpillars feed on exclusively. Look for them in unmowed fields, prairie remnants, and the grassy borders of woodlands where both nectar flowers and host grasses thrive together.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, but peak activity hasn't started yet. Early individuals may be seen nectaring on spring wildflowers if the weather is warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight season with adults most active and visible. This is the best time to spot them visiting white, pink, and purple flowers throughout sunny meadows and field edges.
seasonality.fall: Activity decreases significantly as adults complete their lifecycle. Late-season individuals may still be spotted on warm days visiting late-blooming flowers like asters.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity - the species overwinters in an immature stage, likely as eggs or young caterpillars hidden among grass stems.

funFact: Despite being called 'little glassywing,' these butterflies are actually incredibly picky eaters as caterpillars - they will only eat one type of grass, purpletop grass, making them completely dependent on this single plant species for their entire lifecycle!
confusionNotes: Little glassywings can be confused with other small, brown skippers, but those translucent wing patches are your best clue - most other skippers have solid wing patterns or different types of spots. Remember: if you see those little 'glass windows' catching the light, you've found your little glassywing.
contextualKnowledge: The little glassywing belongs to the skipper family, which gets its name from their distinctive bouncing, 'skipping' flight pattern that's quite different from the smooth gliding of other butterflies. Skippers are actually considered an intermediate group between butterflies and moths, sharing characteristics of both.
compareHints: Since the little glassywing is the only Vernia species in our region, compare it to other small brown skippers like the least skipper or European skipper. The little glassywing's translucent wing spots are unique - other small skippers typically have white or yellow spots that aren't see-through. The little glassywing is also generally more robust-bodied than the delicate least skipper.
